claims.text: The overall tribo-corrosion degradation of high-entropy alloys is governed by the balance between mechanical removal and chemical reformation of a passivating oxide film.
An intact passivating oxide layer protects the alloy against corrosion.
An intact passivating oxide layer protects the alloy against wear.
Mechanical disruption of the oxide film exposes fresh alloy material to rapid corrosion.
Faster oxide-film reformation mitigates both wear and corrosion degradation.
The initial alloy surface has a stable and protective passivating oxide film.
Controlled sliding in a corrosive environment induces continuous oxide-film removal and reformation.
Minor alloying or surface treatment can be used to accelerate oxide-reformation kinetics.
Tribological action mechanically disrupts the protective oxide and momentarily exposes the underlying metal.
The exposed underlying metal undergoes rapid corrosion while the oxide layer reforms in parallel.
Faster oxide reformation lowers net degradation by reducing the time for which unprotected metal is exposed.
Slower oxide reformation produces greater total degradation.
Relative to the baseline, enhanced oxide-reformation kinetics will reduce total degradation.
Relative to the baseline, enhanced oxide-reformation kinetics will reduce wear-volume loss.
Relative to the baseline, enhanced oxide-reformation kinetics will reduce the corrosion rate.
The predicted benefit should occur when oxide-film reformation is rate-limiting for degradation.
The predicted benefit may fail in inert or non-corrosive environments.
The predicted benefit may be minimized when degradation is dominated by mechanical wear or intrinsic bulk properties.
Modified and unmodified specimens should be tested under identical sliding and corrosive conditions as a controlled comparison.
A lack of statistically significant reduction in total degradation, or a failure of the wear and corrosion contributions to change as predicted, is proposed to falsify the hypothesis.
